stories.topic: The 'Naadaan Baalak' at the Export-Target Meeting
stories.summary: Soon after joining the Ministry of Finance, Ajay attended the annual meeting where officials set India's export target. He asked who in the room actually did any exporting. Exporting is done by private people, he said, so the government's real target should be which rules it removed so those people could export. The senior officials treated him like a 'naadaan baalak' (naive child) and told him he would understand the importance of targets once he grew up and became a real policymaker.
stories.insight: The central-planner reflex runs so deep that the state sets targets for activity it does not perform and waves away the obvious objection as immaturity. The useful question for government is what it got out of the way, not what number it announced.
stories.quote: I was like the only child in the room saying, like who in this room does any exporting? Exporting is done by private people. Who are people in this room to make up a target?

stories.topic: Jaswant Singh's 25-Year Dream: Bombay Must Challenge London
stories.summary: When Jaswant Singh was Finance Minister, he sat with Rakesh Mohan and Ajay and asked whether they had thought about Bombay as a global producer of financial services. He said it would take 25 years but that Bombay had to challenge London. Ajay says the idea came from the minister, not from them. It led to Percy Mistry's government committee report 'Bombay as an International Financial Centre' (2007), which ultimately led to FSLRC and a draft law. The report argued that Bombay already has the raw material, including derivatives traders everywhere, deals struck in coffee shops and global banks like JP Morgan with perhaps 60,000 staff in India. What it needed was correct financial regulation and a livable, expat-friendly city that could attract 100,000 top global professionals, down to police stations that can deal with them in English. Then everything got derailed.
stories.insight: A single good question from a politician can launch a decades-long reform programme, and such programmes can just as easily stall. Becoming a financial centre is a long institutional and urban project, and Ajay says the next generation has to pick up the pieces.
stories.quote: And he said, I know this will take twenty-five years, but you have to play for twenty-five years. And Bombay must challenge London.

stories.topic: Percy Mistry Punctures a Young Technologist's Pride
stories.summary: As a young man, Ajay was proud that NSE had the best computer technology in the world and thought it could serve global customers. Percy Mistry told him that was nowhere near enough. Someone holding a two-month dollar-yen futures position in Chicago sleeps soundly because of a whole machinery of private institutions, regulators and law that guarantees the promise. A microphone is different: once made and tested, nobody cares where it came from. Ajay notes NSE once had a real technology edge, but the West has since caught up.
stories.insight: Technology is not the moat in financial services. Institutions are. A financial product is a promise that lasts over time, so buying it means trusting the country that stands behind it.
stories.quote: As a young naive person, I was very comfortable and very proud that at NSE we had the best computer technology in the world, and so we were ready to do this for others in the world and Percy taught me all this. He said, No, hold on, you need much more.

stories.summary: In 2019, a dispute between NSE and SEBI led to a payment delay to foreign participants on NSE. Jayanth Varma wrote a blog post about it. Reading it, Ajay remembered Percy's lesson. The reason for the failure does not matter. On that day the foreigner concludes that payments from a third-world exchange cannot be trusted, and rebuilding that goodwill can take 25 years.
stories.insight: Trust in financial infrastructure takes decades to build and one bad day to lose. An institution must have the competence to make sure 'the show goes on' no matter what the internal dispute is.
stories.quote: You can't have a payment failure at NSE. It doesn't matter why it happened.

stories.topic: Sharad Joshi's Couplet on the APMC Squeeze
stories.summary: Amit recalled the farmer leader Sharad Joshi, one of the few post-independence politicians he truly admires because Joshi cared about freedom. Joshi attacked the APMCs, which had a state-granted monopoly to buy from the farmer at one rupee and sell to the consumer at twenty, leaving neither side any choice. He summed it up in a sher: 'Marte hum bhi hain, marte tum bhi ho. Hum sasta bech ke marte hain, tum mehenga khareed ke marte ho.'
stories.insight: A state-granted middleman monopoly does not trade off the farmer against the consumer. It hurts both at once, and a single couplet captures what pages of policy analysis argue.
stories.quote: I die, my friend, and so do you. I sell my produce cheap and die. You pay too much and you die too.

recommendations.item: Worldly Philosopher: The Odyssey of Albert O. Hirschman
recommendations.creator: Jeremy Adelman
recommendations.context: Raised while introducing Hirschman's 'linkages' idea, and again in the closing recommendations.
recommendations.reason: Hirschman was far more than an economist: a thinker and political philosopher who, in Ajay's words, 'led the world's best life'. If you want to lead a good life, this is the life to study. Ajay says he loves Hirschman as much as he loves James C. Scott.

recommendations.item: The books of Albert O. Hirschman
recommendations.creator: Albert O. Hirschman
recommendations.context: Ajay's closing recommendation, right after spending the episode critiquing Hirschman's linkages argument.
recommendations.reason: Hirschman wasn't wrong about linkages; they simply moved beyond national borders. Thinkers aren't obliged to be precisely correct fifty years later, and Ajay calls him 'one of the great people' whose books and biography everyone should read.

recommendations.creator: Albert O. Hirschman
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation, prompted by Ajay's praise of Hirschman.
recommendations.reason: It is the only Hirschman book Amit has read, and he would love to recommend it. Ajay's enthusiasm convinced Amit to go read Hirschman's other work, and he urges listeners to do the same.

recommendations.item: What Ails Indian Manufacturing? (Ep 104, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Part 1 of this two-parter, recapped in the intro.
recommendations.reason: It covers why Indian manufacturing is in a bad state: eight ways manufacturing differs from services, twelve things that hobble it in India, and seven state-level items for every state's growth strategy. This episode builds on it, and Amit says 'Do check that out.'

recommendations.item: A petty money dispute holds market to ransom
recommendations.creator: Jayanth R Varma
recommendations.context: Ajay's account of the 2019 payment delay to foreign participants on NSE.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it a 'great blog article' on an episode that shows Percy Mistry's lesson in practice: a financial centre can never let a payment fail, whatever the reason.

recommendations.item: The Power of Moore's Laws (Ep 87, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited when explaining Wright's Law and experience curves.
recommendations.reason: That episode centres on Wright's Law, the idea that you get better and cheaper as you do things more. Old development economists wrongly claimed this happens only in manufacturing.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Education (Ep 54, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited as an earlier case of mistaking correlation for causation.
recommendations.reason: The global obsession with schooling first grew out of a correlation: rich England had lots of schooling. Rich countries end up with universal schooling, but schooling isn't what makes them rich.

recommendations.item: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? (Ep 55, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Another example in the 'correlations are not exploitable' series.
recommendations.reason: It shows diminishing returns: a Bombay-Delhi road makes sense, a Bombay-Nagpur road less so. Telecom liberalisation produced the services export revolution, but recent infrastructure spending hasn't solved manufacturing.

recommendations.item: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Ep 56, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited alongside the education and infrastructure episodes.
recommendations.reason: Rich-country governments use more computers, but putting more computers into a poor country's government isn't progress. It is the same correlation trap.

recommendations.item: Don't Mess With the Exchange Rate (Ep 67, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited while explaining why subsidised exports are fake exports.
recommendations.reason: The market should choose the exchange rate. A government can rig it so that even the most incompetent manufacturer looks globally competitive, but that is a transfer from poor people to exporters, not real export strength.

recommendations.item: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Ep 18, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited in the food and agriculture chapter and in the lessons.
recommendations.reason: The case for getting a price system to work and the government out of the way in farming. Then private entrepreneurs will work out things like growing lychees in Bihar to sell in Tokyo.

recommendations.item: The Journey of Indian Finance (Ep 71, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited when explaining how the Bombay financial-centre project stalled after FSLRC.
recommendations.reason: It tells how Indian financial reform got badly stuck, which is the backstory to why the Bombay-as-financial-centre dream remains unfinished.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit invoked the phrase after Ajay's Bombay financial-centre story, predicting it will title a future seminal book by Ajay.
recommendations.reason: Advanced economies run on an invisible infrastructure of institutions and norms that makes everything work smoothly. India needs that, not just the stadium.

recommendations.item: Beware of Industrial Policy (Ep 89, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes; this episode repeatedly restates that industrial policy works badly.
recommendations.reason: It is the fuller case against the state picking winners, which this episode extends to picking among whole sectors.

recommendations.item: Poker and Life (Ep 38, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes after Ajay teases that Amit hangs out with poker people while he hangs out with derivatives traders.
recommendations.reason: For listeners curious about the poker side of the poker-versus-derivatives banter, this is the hosts' episode on what poker teaches about life.

recommendations.item: The Indian State Is the Greatest Enemy of the Indian Farmer
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside the food and agriculture chapter and Amit's Sharad Joshi story.
recommendations.reason: Amit's own piece, which pairs with Sharad Joshi's critique of state-backed APMC monopolies that squeeze both farmers and consumers.

core_ideas.concept: The Four Pillars of the Old Manufacturing Dogma
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay rebuilds the development economics of the 1960s to 1980s from four ideas. (1) Nicholas Kaldor saw that manufacturing growth was correlated with GDP growth. (2) Wright's Law, the experience curve, was claimed to apply only to manufacturing: make 10^8 ball bearings and you get far more productive. (3) Albert Hirschman's linkages: one factory sparks many others, so the state should deliberately induce 'unbalanced growth' and light a few candles to start the chain. (4) Hollis Chenery's World Bank data showed a 'structural transformation' in which successful countries pass through a phase of 20 to 50 percent of GDP in manufacturing before becoming services economies. Together these became a dogma that manufacturing is a mandatory stage, and many economists were willing to use state power to fake it.
core_ideas.quote: Every development success will go through this script, that you will have to go through a manufacturing phase. It is seen as a necessary way station, and then you can graduate to other things.

core_ideas.concept: Hirschman Was Right About Linkages, but Linkages Went Global
core_ideas.explanation: Linkages are real, but they no longer stop at national borders. A 'German' car has seats from the Czech Republic, wiring from Romania and operating-system software from KPIT in Pune. In a world of global value chains, the right policy is not to seed domestic factories. It is to remove every friction against deep global integration: passports, visas, PMLA, the Enforcement Directorate, cross-border payments, and current and capital account restrictions.
core_ideas.quote: Cars are made all over the world and there is no country anymore.

core_ideas.explanation: A recurring Everything is Everything theme. Rich countries have universal schooling, good infrastructure, computerised governments and, historically, manufacturing booms. Sloppy thinking turns these correlations into theories of change and mobilises huge resources around them. Nehru saw lots of schooling in England and pushed schooling first. Ajay argues that what drives growth is peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice. Then private firms build complex, high-productivity businesses over a hundred-year journey, and the correlates follow.
core_ideas.quote: Just because you see a correlation, it's not exploitable.

core_ideas.explanation: Subsidise anything and it will grow, but that isn't growth. A rigged exchange rate makes the most incompetent manufacturer look globally competitive, which amounts to a transfer from poor people to exporters. Real manufacturing has to emerge organically, from self-interested people choosing it because it is optimal for them, not because the state tipped the scales.
core_ideas.quote: If you subsidize something, it will grow. But that's not growth.

core_ideas.concept: Don't Pick Winners Among Sectors: Lay Foundations and Stay Neutral
core_ideas.explanation: The state should fix everything that hobbles manufacturing, agriculture and services alike, then stay neutral. Ranking sectors (manufacturing good, agriculture bad, services unimportant) is central planning, and it keeps poor countries poor for longer. Amit stresses the point is not anti-manufacturing. It is anti-coercion: the trouble starts when the state declares one path to growth and uses force to favour it. The state's job is peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice.
core_ideas.quote: There is a role for the state, which is to lay foundations and then be neutral.

core_ideas.concept: Modern Manufacturing Is a High-Skill Game
core_ideas.explanation: The image of vast factories absorbing unskilled villagers is gone. Modern manufacturing means automation, capital intensity and CNC lathes programmed by English speakers who read manuals and watch YouTube guides. It also needs industrial discipline: showing up at 9 a.m. and working correctly for eight hours, because hundreds of people share an assembly line. Ajay flags a real problem with young Indian men here, a culture of machismo, alcohol, violence and late nights.
core_ideas.quote: There is only a high-skilled game that is available, and we have to play that game.

core_ideas.concept: The Line Between Manufacturing and Services Has Dissolved
core_ideas.explanation: Rolls-Royce doesn't sell engines; it bills by the engine-hour and handles maintenance, remote diagnostics, finance and insurance. A John Deere tractor downloads firmware, probes the soil and sends telemetry to a Hyderabad call centre, which phones the farmer about an infestation. In Ajay's words it is a 'sensor platform', an agricultural productivity service. Kirit Parikh, Ajay's mentor, explained the rise of services long ago: once basic needs are met, people pay for skill and design.
core_ideas.quote: Once you have enough food to eat, you want the best chef to make the food. And that's services.

core_ideas.concept: Services Are Now More Tradable Than Goods, and India Proves It
core_ideas.explanation: Manufacturing was once special because it was tradable. Ajay's father told him haircuts aren't tradable, while widgets are. Fibre-optic cables changed that: a Chicago exchange takes orders from the whole world, and the remaining barriers, such as restrictions on foreign lawyers and accountants, are only in our minds. Over ten years, India's goods exports grew 38% in nominal dollars, roughly half a percent a year after US inflation, while services exports grew 126%. Ajay calls India 'ground zero' where the old theory is being destroyed. Services exports, about $300 billion a year from a small educated elite, are what separate India from Pakistan and Bangladesh.
core_ideas.quote: But if you are able to solve the cobwebs of your brain, services today are more tradable than goods because of the availability of modern fiber optic cables.

core_ideas.concept: A Financial Product Is Only as Good as Its Institutions
core_ideas.explanation: Percy Mistry's lesson. Once a microphone is made and tested, where it came from no longer matters. A two-month dollar-yen futures position leaves you exposed, for those two months, to how the whole system around it works: checks and balances, conflict resolution, regulators and law. Exporting financial services therefore means exporting trustworthy institutions, which is far harder than having good technology.
core_ideas.quote: Percy said the quality of the financial product is the quality of its institutional environment.

core_ideas.explanation: Build the world's finest stadiums, Wankhede or Brabourne, and top teams still won't come if the umpires are shady. Ajay credits Britain's success at Wimbledon, where foreigners always win, to the same idea. Britain built the rules of the game and won the world's trust that British common law will deliver and that the unwritten constitution prevents the excesses of state power. Getting to the top in services is an institutional challenge, not a matter of machines.
core_ideas.quote: It's not the technical characteristics of the stadium. The umpires are key.

core_ideas.concept: Norms: The Layer Beneath the Law
core_ideas.explanation: Good behaviour by umpires and judges isn't produced by statute alone. An umpire should feel embarrassed when friends ask what on earth he was doing. Judges behave better when researchers write blog posts criticising their orders. Building institutions requires a culture of respect, scrutiny and constant striving to do better.
core_ideas.quote: Umpires are not made just by law. They're made by people. They're made by respect.

core_ideas.concept: Agriculture Is a Frontier of Productivity, Not a Backwater
core_ideas.explanation: The Netherlands, roughly the size of Haryana or Kerala, is the world's third-largest food exporter at about $140 billion a year. Modern agriculture means indoor farming, agri-robots and genetic engineering, run by skilled people rather than unskilled peasants. Ajay says the world economy pays for complexity: getting lychees from Bihar to Tokyo is complex, and private people worked that trade out, not the government. India's food exports (about $43 billion) already exceed its textile and apparel exports (about $34 billion).
core_ideas.quote: Agriculture is only low grade if your imagination is low grade.

core_ideas.concept: The East Asian Miracle Is Not a Model
core_ideas.explanation: Many people are 'taken by', and in Ajay's view 'taken in by', the East Asian miracle. A rare kind of developmental dictatorship pushed manufacturing and got growth, but Ajay 'wouldn't wish it on my worst enemies'. Those countries are not admirable examples to emulate, and the world has changed since then anyway.
core_ideas.quote: As I always say, that if China is so great, how come your kid doesn't want to migrate to China?

core_ideas.concept: The Intellectual Map Lags the Territory
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's framing of why manufacturing dogma survives. The world changes faster than the people who think about it, and conventional wisdom catches up slowly. Ajay's two lessons for young economists: be very cautious about correlation versus causation, and distrust any leadership role for the state in choosing society's path.
core_ideas.quote: The map of the world is always out of date, but in the world of intellectual constructs, it's much more out of date than you would otherwise expect.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on Ajay's cooling temper between the off-camera rant and the recording: 'Ten minutes ago, before we started the shoot, he was using words like rage and fury. He was then a volcano. He is now a flickering candle. But it doesn't matter because you will still get the light and insight.'

Ajay's opening salvo: 'Development economists are a bit of a creepy bunch. They are statist control people, and they have long had this smug comfort and superiority complex that they get to control the world.'

Right after Ajay's lyrical riff on John Deere tractors as sensor platforms, Amit tries a groaner pun: 'If you are a man who gets turned on by farm vehicles, what would those vehicles be called?' Ajay's verdict: 'Brilliant.'

Ajay's test for a real financial centre: 'You throw a stone at any residential building in Bombay, and you will hit some derivatives trader.' He then ribs Amit: 'I know you hang out with the people who do conversations about poker, but I hang out with the people who do conversations about derivatives trading.'

Amit on the roller coaster of Ajay's example: being invited to imagine a thousand-crore dollar-yen futures position felt great, since 'I have never traded in futures or options, and I have much closer to a thousand rupees than a thousand crores. But much, much closer.' Then the poker jibe brought him crashing down.
Amit's hasty disclaimer after the 'shady umpires' analogy: 'When he talks about umpires, he is not implying that Indian umpires are bad. Indian umpires are the best umpires.'

Prompted by the Netherlands being the size of Haryana, Amit recalls Iceland drawing 1-1 with Argentina at the 2018 World Cup. He calculated from his study that Iceland's population is the size of Versova: 'Not Bombay, not Andheri, not even Andheri West, because Andheri is vast and contains multitudes. But freaking Versova. So from this we can come to the conclusion that football and food have more in common than you think.' Ajay adds: 'Iceland is three hundred thousand fishermen.'

Amit reveals Ajay's 'metric for goodness': the fraction of Everything is Everything episodes you've watched. 'At noon every Friday, even if you were hundred percent good at eleven fifty-nine, you get a little less good because a new episode is out,' but watching at 3x speed lets you catch up fast. 'So my question for you, dear listeners, is: are you good?'
Nicholas Kaldor's 'laws of growth': his 1950s observation that manufacturing growth tracks GDP growth, the first pillar of the manufacturing dogma.
Wright's Law and experience curves: the more you produce, the more productive you get. Old development economists wrongly assumed this applied only to manufacturing.
Albert O. Hirschman's 'linkages' and 'unbalanced growth': the argument that the state should deliberately spark a few industries so that capitalist incentives fill in the rest.

Hollis Chenery's 'structural transformation': built on the first high-quality multi-country development datasets at the World Bank, it held that every successful economy passes through a manufacturing-heavy phase.
Nehru's schooling push: Ajay says Nehru saw lots of schooling in England and concluded India needed lots of schooling, a classic case of mistaking a correlate of wealth for its cause.
Japan's MITI: 'For every one Japanese MITI that did some good things, I can show you 50 other examples where industrial policy went wrong.'
Wimbledon: 'The British organized Wimbledon and foreigners always win at Wimbledon. That's the glory of Britain,' credited to rule of law and the world's trust in British common law.
James C. Scott: Ajay says he loves Hirschman as much as he loves James C. Scott.
